cards.text: Welcome in, friend. This book opens with the words of a man it calls the Teacher, a king in Jerusalem. And let me tell you, he does NOT ease into it.

cards.question: The Teacher, king in Jerusalem, is the son of ___.
Right away, the Teacher says only some things are futile.

cards.text: EVERYTHING, friend. He doesn't even say good morning. Just futility of futilities, TWICE, in case somebody in the back missed it, and then a question about all the labor a man toils at under the sun.

cards.question: The Teacher looks at all the labor a person toils at under the sun. What does he ask about it?

answers.text: What a man gains from it
How long a man must keep at it
Who a man is working for

cards.text: Then he zooms WAY out and looks at people across time. Generations come, and generations go.

cards.question: While the generations come and go, the Teacher says the ___ remains forever.
Then the Teacher points up: the sun rises and the sun sets. What does he say it does after it sets?

answers.text: Hurries back to where it rises

cards.text: Then the Teacher turns to the wind, blowing southward and then turning northward. That wind has my sense of direction, friend.

cards.question: The Teacher watches the wind blow southward, then turn northward. What does he say it keeps doing?
All the rivers flow into the sea, and the Teacher says the sea finally fills up.
All the rivers flow into the sea. Where does the Teacher say the streams flow again?

answers.text: Back to the place they came from

cards.text: Then the Teacher says all things are wearisome, more than one can describe. Friend, I spent years in a junk drawer counting dust, and I STILL couldn't describe it.

cards.question: The Teacher says all things are wearisome, more than one can describe. He says the eye and the ear never get ___.

cards.text: Then the Teacher looks at what has been and what has been done, and says it will all be done again. Stamp, bake, box, repeat: that's my whole week, and I LOVE it.

cards.question: The Teacher says there is nothing ___ under the sun.

cards.text: Nothing new. So what about when somebody points at something and says, "Look, this is new"?

cards.question: Someone points at a thing and calls it new. The Teacher says it already existed in the ages before us.

cards.text: Then the Teacher says there is no remembrance of those who came before. Friend, after years in the back of a junk drawer, I don't need that one explained.

cards.question: The Teacher also talks about being remembered. He says people yet to come will be remembered by those who follow after them.

findings.problem: No story card sets up verse 2 before this question. The word 'futile' first shows up in the question itself, and the only hint before it is card 1's 'he does NOT ease into it.' Without the title, which doesn't count, the baker has nothing in the cards to reason from about what the Teacher says is futile. A story card telling the Teacher's opening cry needs to come before this card, or the question should change.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences: 'EVERYTHING, friend.' / 'He doesn't even say good morning.' / 'Just futility of futilities, TWICE, … under the sun.' Only the opening card may run to three.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The wrong answer 'Up into the clouds above' is arguable. Many readers take verse 7's water returning to the place it came from as the water cycle through the clouds, so a baker could argue this answer is right. It needs a wrong answer that is clearly false.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The wrong answer 'tired' is arguable. 'The eye and the ear never get tired' is a common way to say they keep wanting more, which is close to 'not satisfied with seeing, nor … content with hearing' (Ecclesiastes 1:8). A baker could argue it's right.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: All four fill-in-the-blank cards (2, 7, 14, 16) put the blank on the last word of the sentence. Where the blank falls has become a pattern instead of a natural choice for each card.

rule.text: No formula. Which question type comes next, the order the types come in and where a blank falls are chosen naturally for each card. They never follow a pattern.
